scenes.tts: Some systems are too tangled to reason about in words. Two feedback loops, a delay, or a crowd of competing cells can behave in ways intuition does not predict. And a measured curve cannot say why it has its shape. A model proposes a cause, and makes a number that the cause must produce.
scenes.visual: Tangled network of loops, a delay and a crowd of cells with a question mark; then a measured curve marked example with a question, and a model box that sends a predicted number onto it.

scenes.tts: First, state the assumptions, including what is left out. The classical predator-prey model assumes prey grow exponentially without predators. Consumption is proportional to prey times predators. There is no handling time. And each predator dies at a constant rate.
scenes.visual: An assumptions box fills line by line while a prey and predator sketch builds; handling time is drawn crossed out as left out.
scenes.narration: First, state the assumptions, including what is left out. The classical predator-prey model assumes prey grow exponentially without predators. Consumption is proportional to prey times predators. There is no handling time. And each predator dies at a constant rate.

scenes.tts: Second, write the rules as an equation. Exponential growth is d N by d t equals r N. Logistic growth is r N times one minus N over K. Growth per individual falls in a straight line with N. Total growth peaks at half of K. And K is an equilibrium, not a ceiling.
scenes.visual: Equations on the left, growth curves computed from them on the right; then per-individual growth as a straight line and total growth as a hump peaking at K/2, crossing zero at K.
scenes.caption: Second, write the rules as an equation. Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN. Logistic growth is rN(1 − N/K). Growth per individual falls in a straight line with N. Total growth peaks at half of K. And K is an equilibrium, not a ceiling.
scenes.narration: Second, write the rules as an equation. Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN. Logistic growth is rN(1 − N/K). Growth per individual falls in a straight line with N. Total growth peaks at half of K. And K is an equilibrium, not a ceiling.

scenes.tts: Third, run it. The predator-prey equations give repeating cycles that neither grow nor shrink, with predator peaks lagging prey peaks. Now change one assumption and run it again. Make prey growth logistic, and the cycles change. Check which conclusions survive a changed assumption.
scenes.visual: Computed prey and predator curves cycle with a marked lag; the plot shrinks to the top and a rerun with logistic prey growth is drawn below.

scenes.tts: Then compare with data the model was not fitted to. Hodgkin and Huxley fitted their squid axon model to separate current measurements. For one fibre at eighteen point five degrees Celsius, the nineteen fifty-two equations predicted conduction at eighteen point eight metres a second. The measurement was twenty-one point two. Study that gap. Where a model fails shows what to test next.
scenes.visual: Separate current measurements feed fitted equations; two lanes race a pulse, predicted 18.8 then measured 21.2; the gap is marked and prompts tests of assumptions, parameters and measurements.

scenes.tts: A fit is not a mechanism. Several curves with different assumptions can fit the same points. Hodgkin and Huxley's n to the fourth was a fit to data, not a count of channel parts. So test predictions and assumptions, not fit alone. And competitive exclusion is predicted with one limiting resource, a constant environment, and no other check on the winner. List the conditions with the conclusion.
scenes.visual: Example points with two different curves through them; the n to the fourth note; then competitive exclusion with its three conditions and the two controls.

scenes.tts: The Hodgkin and Huxley equations of nineteen fifty-two described the currents. They did not prove a gating mechanism. The conductance model of squid axon computed the action potential and the conduction speed, and a historical review credits it with predicting features of channel gating before channels could be seen. In the nineteen thirties, Gause grew two Paramecium species. Alone, each followed roughly logistic curves. Mixed, aurelia persisted and caudatum declined in his cultures. It was a laboratory test of the Lotka-Volterra theory of competition.
scenes.visual: Left: a spike computed from the conductance model, 1952; right: two species alone then mixed, computed from the competition equations, 1930s.

scenes.tts: In 1996, Huang and Ferrell solved the rate equations of the M A P K cascade. The model predicted ultrasensitivity, a Hill coefficient of four to five, though no cooperative enzyme was assumed. Oocyte extracts matched. In 2008, Deppmann and colleagues simulated neurons competing for N G F made at a constant rate. Neurons separated into winners and losers only with feedback on T r k A level and on signal duration. The predictions were tested in mouse ganglia. Keep this rule. A good fit does not show that the equation's mechanism is the one at work.
scenes.visual: Left: Hill curves computed for n of 4 to 5 versus n = 1, no cooperativity; right: neurons share a fixed supply and separate under two feedbacks; then the rule alone.
